title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Mason residents win a town hall while Kalamazoo and Ypsilanti hit pause on new projects.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're digging into why Mason just approved a communication plan instead of rushing approvals, and how that fits into the growing pushback from towns across the state.
Emmy, the lead story is out of Ingham County where Mason City Council unanimously passed the Mason Connect plan last night.
Right, and residents packed the meeting to voice concerns about noise, traffic, and higher electricity costs from a proposed facility nearby.
Instead of moving straight to approvals, the council set up a Sept. 14 town hall plus neighborhood meetings to keep everyone updated on any future proposals.
That feels like a direct response to the strong public opposition during comment period. What does this tell us about how these projects are landing in smaller communities?
It shows even mid-sized towns like Mason are now facing the same pressures we've seen in Kalamazoo and Ypsilanti Township.
Graham, walk me through the bigger picture here. Why are so many places suddenly hitting the brakes on data centers?

The core issues are the same everywhere: these facilities need enormous amounts of power and water, they run 24/7 so noise is constant, and they can strain local roads with construction and maintenance traffic.
And the power piece seems especially big right now with data centers driving load growth across the Lower Peninsula.
Exactly. Michigan's utility regulator is already looking at changes to how new transmission lines and substations get paid for, and ratepayers could see that show up on monthly bills.
So if a town approves one of these, does that mean higher rates for everyone in the region, or just locally?
It tends to ripple out because the grid is interconnected. That's why folks 30 miles away in other counties are starting to pay attention.
And water use is another flashpoint, right? These places can pull millions of gallons a day for cooling.
Yes, and in places like Coldwater they just held an informational session yesterday laying out the exact numbers on power demand, water needs, and what tax revenue might look like in return.
So residents are getting concrete trade-off data now instead of vague promises.
That's the shift. Branch County folks heard about potential jobs versus infrastructure strain at that meeting, and similar conversations are happening in Mason.
What about the history here? Has Michigan seen this kind of rapid developer interest before?

Not at this scale. The University of Michigan just locked in a $1.2 billion site in Ypsilanti Township yesterday despite local objections, and now the township is weighing a moratorium on power line upgrades to slow things down.
That moratorium vote is actually happening today, correct?
Yes, Ypsilanti Township Board of Trustees meets tonight on a six-month pause specifically aimed at data center transmission infrastructure.
And Kalamazoo just enacted a full one-year moratorium on new data centers and battery plants after residents raised alarms about noise, power, and water.
Kalamazoo joins a growing list of communities trying to buy time to write permanent zoning rules that could limit where these facilities can go.
So the pattern is clear: public meetings, organized opposition, then local governments stepping in with pauses or communication plans.
And in Mason the council chose the outreach route instead of a moratorium, at least for now.
What happens next in Mason specifically?
The Sept. 14 town hall will be the first big public update, and they'll hold neighborhood meetings in between to answer questions directly.
That seems like a smart way to keep the conversation going instead of letting it turn into a standoff.
It also gives officials time to gather more details on exactly what any proposal would require from the grid and local services.
Meanwhile, state-level tension is rising too. Attorney General Dana Nessel is fighting to close the Campbell coal plant even as data centers increase electricity demand.
Keeping that plant running longer means continued emissions and costs that ratepayers would shoulder, according to her challenge of the latest federal order.
So the data center boom is colliding with the state's broader energy transition goals.
That's the tension. More load growth makes it harder to retire older plants on the original timeline.
And this isn't just Ingham County anymore. Coldwater, Kalamazoo, Ypsilanti, Mason, they're all dealing with versions of the same question.
Right, and developers are eyeing more southwest Michigan sites after the Coldwater session gave them a clearer picture of what's possible.
For listeners in mid-Michigan or even farther out, why should they care about what's happening in Mason today?
Because similar proposals are surfacing in townships across the region, and the decisions made in one place can affect power rates and water availability for neighbors 30 or 60 miles away.
The infrastructure doesn't stop at the town line.
Exactly. That's why these local fights are starting to feel statewide.
Let's move to a couple quick hits. Kalamazoo's one-year moratorium just went into effect after residents pushed back hard.
Yes, and officials there now have time to draft permanent rules that could restrict where large-scale projects can locate.
Meanwhile in Coldwater, residents got their first detailed look at the numbers on power use, water demand, and potential tax revenue yesterday.
That session came as more developers scout southwest Michigan, so folks there are getting ahead of the curve with real data.
And over in Ypsilanti Township, they're weighing that moratorium on power transmission upgrades specifically to stall the U-M project.
The university confirmed the $1.2 billion location yesterday, but local officials say they'll keep fighting it.
State regulators are also eyeing rate changes tied to all this new demand, which could hit bills across the Lower Peninsula.
Those proposed changes would alter how utilities recover costs for new lines and substations needed to serve the data centers.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to show up.
Tonight the Ypsilanti Township Board of Trustees will vote on that six-month moratorium on power transmission infrastructure for data centers.
And the Village of Morley Board meets tonight too for a data center proposal discussion and possible vote.
Those are the two big ones happening today that people can actually attend.
Anything else we should flag for tomorrow or later this week?
The Mason town hall is scheduled for Sept. 14, so that's the next big public forum in Ingham County.
Plenty for folks to keep an eye on.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Mason Approves Outreach Plan as Data Center Pushback Spreads Across Michigan
